.5. It is stated that respondent No. 3 was appointed as the competent authority.

The respondent No.3 vide award dated 30.03.2011 determined the market value of agricultural lands at Rs.
2,25,00,000/- per acre and non-agricultural lands at Rs. 1,314/- per sq. feet.

In order to determine the market value, the respondent No.3 obtained the sale statistics for the period from 08.12.2008 to 09.12.2009 as well as guidance values for the relevant period of the said village from the office of the Sub-Registrar, Bengaluru North Taluka.
The respondent No.3 observed that the average of the sale statistics was Rs. 1,75,02,857/- per acre, whereas, the guidance value was Rs.1,75,00,000/- per acre.

The respondent No. 3 relied upon the guidance values which was higher than sale statistics and determined the market value of agricultural lands at Rs. 2,25,00,000/- per acre equivalent to Rs.
5,559.86/- per sq. meters in so far as NA lands were concerned, the respondent no.3 observed that the average of the sale statistics was Rs. 533/- per sq. feet and the guidance value was Rs. 500/- per sq. feet.

Both the average of the sale statistics as well as the guidance value was found by respondent No. 3 to be on a lower A.P. No.76/2022 side, Rs. 1,314/- per sq. feet was fixed as the guidance value of NA lands situated in Venkatala village.

sentences.text: It is stated that being dissatisfied with the amount awarded by respondent No. 3, the respondent No. 1 approached the respondent No. 2 under Section 3-G(5) of the NH Act.
The petitioner entered appearance and filed its statement of objections with documents as well as written submissions with several judgments in support of its defence.

The respondent No.2 has enhanced the market value from Rs. 516.71 per sq. feet to Rs. 2,625/- per sq. feet treating the subject lands as NA.

Being aggrieved by the impugned Arbitral Award, the petitioner has preferred this petition on the following grounds.
1) It is stated that the impugned Arbitral Award passed by the respondent No.2 is perverse, patently illegal, capricious and goes against the very fundamentals of A & C Act.

of the award has observed the respondent No. 1 has produced the copy of the official memorandum bearing No. ALN(317)/98-99 dated 15.10.1998 passed by the Deputy Commissioner, Bengaluru District wherein, the lands have been converted for NA (Res) purposes and accordingly the lands are treated as NA.
In fact no such document was served upon the petitioner at any point of time which is contrary to Section 24(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act.

3) Without even ascertaining the actual extent of conversion and in the absence of any proof to the effect that the subject lands fell within the converted extent, the respondent No. 2 has held that the subject lands were NA in nature.
4) The respondent had to examine the original conversion order and no conclusion could be drawn based upon photocopy since the matter involves public money.

5) The respondent No. 2 has taken the guidance value of some other village and A.P. No.76/2022 held that lands in Sy.No. 9 of Yelahanka Amanikere village are abutting NH and then added additional percentage on the guidance value of Venkatala village which is completely erroneous.
6) The respondent No. 2 could not have relied upon a notification which came into effect after a lapse of more than 1 year and 9 months from the date of publication of preliminary notification.
7) The respondent No. 2 has grossly erred in not following the provisions of NH Act i.e., Section 3-G(7)(a), the substantive law while passing the impugned award which is contrary to the provisions of Section 28 of Arbitration and Conciliation Act.
8) The impugned arbitral award is completely illegal and arbitrary and in contravention of Section 3-G(7)(a) of NH Act as well as Section 31(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act.

9) The respondent No. 2 has not assigned any reasons for re-determining the compensation amount at Rs. 2,625/- per sq. feet especially when the parties had neither agreed that no reasons were to be given nor the impugned arbitral award is an award on agreed terms under Section 30 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act.

.15. Section 34(2) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 provide the circumstances under which an award can be set aside by a civil Court.
(2) It is in conflict with contravention with the fundamental policy of Indian Law or iii) It is in conflict with most basic notion of morality or justice.
Explanation 2. The test as to whether there is contravention with the fundamental policy of Indian law shall not entail a review on the merits of the dispute.

2A It may also be set aside if the Court finds the award is vitiated by patent illegality appearing on the face of award A.P. No.76/2022 provided that an award shall not be set aside merely on the ground of an erroneous application of law or by re appreciation of evidence.

.16. In Kwality Manufacturing Corporation Vs. Central Whorehouse Corporation (2009) 5 Sec.142, it has been held that:
"From catena of other judgments of this Court, it is clear that for the objector /
appellant in order to succeed in their challenge against an arbitral award, they must show that the award of the Arbitrator suffered from perversity or an error of law or that the Arbitrator has otherwise misconducted himself.

Bearing in mind the above section and decision, now it has to be seen whether the impugned award suffers from any patent error, illegality as envisaged above.
.17.

The respondent has contended that the petition is filed after 1 year 2 months 11 days and therefore the petition has to be dismissed under Section 34(3) of Arbitration and Conciliation Act.
The Hon'ble Supreme Court in suo-motto case W.P. No. 3 of 2020 has extended the period of limitation on account of Covid-19.

As the petition is filed within the extended period of limitation, it is in time.
.18.

The petitioner has contended that the respondent No. 2 in page No. 5 of the award had observed that the respondent No. 1 had produced copy of the official memorandum bearing No.
ALN(317)/98- 99 dated 15.10.1998 passed by the Deputy Commissioner, Bengaluru District wherein the lands have been converted for NA purpose and accordingly the lands are treated as NA.

sentences.text: From the order sheet maintained by Arbitrator there is no noting with regard to production of conversion order by the respondent No. 1.
Neither in the application seeking for enhancement nor in the written argument filed by the respondent he mentioned about enclosing conversion order.
The respondent No. 3 determined the market value considering the acquired as converted land.
The respondent No. 2 has now by virtue of the award has treated the land as NA land.
The petitioner had no opportunity to have their say on the document.
There is violation of principles of natural justice which amounts to patent illegality.
The petitioner has stated that the respondent No.3 - the Arbitrator has relied upon the notification dated 21.09.2011 which came into effect on 26.09.2011.
Preliminary notification in the present case was issued on 09.12.2009.

It is stated that as per Substantial Law NH Authority Act Section 3-G(7)(a), the arbitrator while determining the amount shall take into consideration the market value of the land as on the date of publication of the notification under Section 3-A of NH Act.

The respondent No.2 could not have relied upon the guidelines value which came into effect after publication of preliminary notification dated 09.12.2009.
.23.

The Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Oil & Natural Gas Corp. Ltd., Vs. SAW Pipes Ltd. (AIR 2003 SC 2629) has held that:
 "if the award is contrary to the  Substantive provisions of law or the provisions of the Act or against the terms of the contract, it would be patently illegal,
which could be interfered under Section 34".

sentences.text: The respondent No. 1 advocate argued that as per Section 2(6) of Arbitration and Conciliation Act the provisions of Section 28(1)(a) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act is not applicable to this case.

As per Sector 2(6) provides that:

sentences.text: From reading of Section 2(6) it is clear that the parties are free to determine a certain issue.
However, A.P. No.76/2022 it is not applicable to Section 28.
The rules prescribed under Section 28 is mandatory.
In view of the said provisions, the contention of the respondent No. 1 is not sustainable.
.26. The Arbitrator relying upon the guidelines value dated 21.09.2011 has redetermined the market value at Rs. 2,625/- per sq. feet.
Entry at Sl. No. 128 at page 463 provides for guidance value of NA land situated at Venkatala village at Rs. 1500/- per sq. feet.
Entry at Sl. No. 118 at page 462 provides for guidance value of NA lands situated at Amanikere village at Rs. 800/- per sq. feet.
The respondent No. 2 has taken guidance value of Rs. 1500/- per sq. feet as the basis for redetermining the market value.
The respondent No. 2 has not assigned reasons as to why he has taken the value of land situated at Venkatala village instead of Yelahanka Amanikere village.

Apart from that the respondent No. 2 has added 50% on the guidance value on the ground that the said lands are abutting to the National Highways and thereafter the respondent No. 2 has once- again added 25% as enhancement on his wisdom.
The respondent No. 2 has not given reasons for adding 25% more on his wisdom when the guidelines do not provide for it.
.27. The respondent No. 1 has contended that award passed by respondent No. 1 is speaking order.

Hence, there was no violation of the order of respondent No. 2 in enhancing award to Rs. 2,625/-
per sq. feet.
The rate for NA lands at Ammanikere village is Rs. 800.
The arbitral award does not say the reason for taking A.P. No.76/2022 the basis as Rs. 1,500/- per sq. feet.
Therefore, the award passed by the Arbitrator is arbitrary.
.28. The Arbitrator has relied upon guidelines value dated 21.09.2011.
This document is not valid record received from the Arbitrator as none of the parties have produced and this is evident from the record of the Arbitrator.
Section 24(3) of the Act provides provision regarding hearing and written proceedings.

It reads thus:
"All statements, documents or other information supplied to, or applications made to the aribral tribunal by one party shall be communicated to the other party, and any expert report or evidentiary document on which the arbital tribunal may rely in making its decision shall be communicated to the parties".

sentences.text: The respondent No. 1 has contended that the provisions of Section 24(1)(2)(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act does not apply to Arbitrator as he is sole Arbitrator.

The provisions of Section 24 is clear that unless other wise agreed by the parties, the Arbitral Tribunal shall decide whether to hold oral hearings for the presentation of evidence or for oral argument, or whether the proceedings shall be conducted on the basis of documents and other materials.
In the present case there is no agreement between the parties.
In the absence of agreement the provisions of Section 24 is applicable to sole arbitrator also.

.30. As the Arbitrator has relied on the estimated guidelines value of immovable properties and buildings dated 21.09.2011 without bringing to the knowledge of the parties and thereby has failed to follow the procedure under Section 24 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act.
So the award has to be set aside on the ground of patent illegality.

.31. The petitioner has contended that the respondent No.2 has not assigned any reasons for re- determining the compensation nor he has assigned any reasons for enhancing the compensation or for relying upon notification dated 21.09.2011.
.32.

In Som Dutt Builders Ltd Vs. State of Kerala (2010)2 AWC (supp) 1390 SC) has held that:
A.P. No.76/2022 "Reasons must be indicated in the award as that would reflect thought process leading to a particular conclusion.

.16. In Kwality Manufacturing Corporation Vs. Central Whorehouse Corporation (2009) 5 Sec.142, it has been held that:
"From catena of other judgments of this Court, it is clear that for the objector /
appellant in order to succeed in their challenge against an arbitral award, they must show that the award of the Arbitrator suffered from perversity or an error of law or that the Arbitrator has otherwise misconducted himself.
Though the learned Arbitrator is not bound by the provisions of the Indian Evidence Act, the principles of the Indian Evidence Act are applicable even in the arbitral proceedings.
The learned Arbitrator could not have relied upon those unproved and disputed documents while rejecting the claims made by the petitioners.
There is violation of principles of natural justice which amounts to patent illegality.
From reading of Section 2(6) it is clear that the parties are free to determine a certain issue.
However, A.P. No.76/2022 it is not applicable to Section 28.
This document is not valid record received from the Arbitrator as none of the parties have produced and this is evident from the record of the Arbitrator.
The respondent No. 1 has contended that the provisions of Section 24(1)(2)(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act does not apply to Arbitrator as he is sole Arbitrator.
The provisions of Section 24 is clear that unless other wise agreed by the parties, the Arbitral Tribunal shall decide whether to hold oral hearings for the presentation of evidence or for oral argument, or whether the proceedings shall be conducted on the basis of documents and other materials.
In the present case there is no agreement between the parties.
In the absence of agreement the provisions of Section 24 is applicable to sole arbitrator also.
So the award has to be set aside on the ground of patent illegality.
